analysis.one_liner: Shields hospitals and doctors from malpractice lawsuits for emergency care by treating them as federal employees.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee in April 2009 and sat there until the Congress ended in January 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Public Health Service Act so that hospitals, emergency departments, and the doctors who work in them — including on-call specialists — are treated as federal Public Health Service employees for malpractice purposes when they provide emergency screening, treatment, and follow-up care required by the EMTALA law [S2][S3]. That means patients injured by negligent emergency care could no longer sue the hospital or doctor in ordinary court for unlimited damages; instead, claims would go through the federal system, where compensation is capped and paid from a federal fund [S3]. The stated goal is to attract more specialists to staff emergency rooms and trauma centers by lowering their insurance costs. The bill was introduced, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospitals and the doctors who staff their emergency rooms would gain federal malpractice protection for emergency and post-stabilization care, lowering their insurance costs. The bill's findings argue this would also help patients by keeping specialists willing to cover emergency departments and trauma centers that have lost coverage due to liability costs [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Hospitals and emergency departments, and physicians who serve them — including on-call specialists with no other tie to the hospital — would be covered by the federal FTCA-style malpractice shield for EMTALA-mandated emergency and post-stabilization care [S2][S3].

The bill's findings argue that liability exposure drives specialists to drop emergency call coverage and that protection would increase coverage, citing IOM, GAO, AHA, and HHS advisory-group reports [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Patients injured by negligent emergency care would bear the cost: they would lose the right to sue for full damages in ordinary court and instead go through a federal claims system with capped awards paid from an appropriated fund [S3]. Taxpayers would ultimately backstop those payments.

drawbacks.text: It would eliminate the right of patients injured by negligent emergency care to sue the hospital or physician in ordinary court, replacing it with the federal system in which recoveries are capped and claims are paid out of a government fund — a real cost for patients who suffer malpractice harm [S3].

The protection would extend beyond the emergency room visit to all post-stabilization services related to the condition, so a wide range of follow-up care would fall under the federal shield, not just the chaotic first moments of emergency treatment [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The malpractice-liability shield is real relief for a genuine problem — specialists avoiding emergency-department call duty because of lawsuit exposure — and it would keep more trauma and emergency coverage available in the places that have lost it. But the design is one-sided: it bars ordinary malpractice lawsuits against emergency providers rather than reforming liability more broadly, and it shifts the cost of emergency-care mistakes from providers and their insurers to the federal government and, indirectly, taxpayers. Patients injured by negligent emergency care would lose their day in court. The bill also never advanced beyond a referral, so neither benefit nor cost was ever realized.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee's Health Subcommittee in April 2009 and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Bart Gordon introduced the bill on April 21, 2009, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1][S5].
The next day it was referred to the Subcommittee on Health, and no further action was ever recorded — no markup, no vote, no floor consideration [S5].
The bill died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, physicians, and their malpractice insurers are better off, because the liability shield that would have limited malpractice claims against emergency care never became law; patients' existing right to sue for negligent emergency care is intact.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients' right to sue for emergency malpractice

for.name: Rep. Charlie Dent
for.what_they_did: Joined the bill as an original cosponsor at introduction [S3].

for.name: 3 of 178 House Republicans and 1 of 253 House Democrats

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Health Subcommittee)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it out during the two-year Congress [S5].

sides.party_line_note: The bill's only five cosponsors split across both parties (1 Democrat and 4 Republicans), and with no votes ever taken there is no record of how the parties lined up.

industries.note: The bill would cap their malpractice exposure for emergency care by routing claims into the federal system, lowering their liability costs. The counterweight is that patients injured by negligence would face a harder, capped path to compensation.

industries.industry: Physicians, especially high-risk specialties like neurosurgery and orthopedics
industries.note: Emergency and on-call physicians would get federal malpractice protection, addressing the liability costs that the bill's findings say keep specialists away from emergency-department call coverage. Their gain comes at the expense of patients' ordinary right to sue for negligence.
The bill would remove emergency-care malpractice cases from the tort system, reducing the ability of injured patients and their attorneys to bring full-value claims against hospitals and physicians.

Malpractice judgments for emergency care would flow through a federal fund subject to annual appropriations rather than private insurers. Taxpayers would indirectly absorb costs that providers' insurers previously bore.
